blocks.text: EV Charging in South Surrey & White Rock: 2026 Guide

parts.t: Posted on
November 18, 2026
by
Jared Gibbons

BC Hydro has rebuilt its South Surrey fast-charging site, so twelve cars can now charge at once where four could before. That makes this a good time to lay out where you can charge on the Peninsula, what it costs, and the question I get from buyers most often: can I charge an EV in this condo or townhome?

blocks.text: The short version

items.t: Fastest public charging: the BC Hydro hub and the Tesla Supercharger, both in the Real Canadian Superstore lot at 2332 160 Street.
BC Hydro's price since April 1, 2026: about 40 cents a kWh at a fast charger and 31 cents at a Level 2 charger, plus GST.
In a strata, you have the right to ask for a charger, and the council has three months to answer and cannot refuse without a good reason.
Buying a condo or townhome: ask for the building's electrical planning report. Most stratas here must have one by December 31, 2026.

blocks.text: Where to fast-charge in South Surrey
BC Hydro hub at the Superstore, 2332 160 Street

parts.t: The site now has six 180 kW chargers. Each one can split its power between two vehicles, so up to twelve can plug in at the same time. The chargers carry CCS, CHAdeMO and NACS (Tesla-style) connectors, and BC Hydro says one can add up to 180 km of range to an average EV in about 10 minutes. The site opened in 2018 with two 50 kW units and gained two 100 kW units in January 2024, so this is its third and biggest version. Source:
BC Hydro bulletin, October 29, 2026

blocks.text: Tesla Supercharger, same parking lot

parts.t: Tesla runs a 12-stall V3 Supercharger in the same Superstore lot, with peak charging of up to 250 kW. Between the two networks, this corner of Grandview is the busiest charging stop on the Peninsula, and it's a few minutes from Highway 99.

blocks.text: South Surrey Park and Ride

parts.t: BC Hydro and TransLink opened a hub at the South Surrey Park and Ride in February 2025, with 180 kW fast chargers and Level 2 chargers. The fast chargers come with one hour of free parking; the Level 2 stalls require paying for parking. It suits commuters who take the bus downtown and want a full battery waiting.

blocks.text: Elsewhere in Surrey and White Rock

parts.t: BC Hydro counts nine other charging sites in Surrey, for 95 ports across the city. In White Rock, charging maps list Level 2 chargers at public parkades near the waterfront, which are slower but fine for a few hours at the beach or dinner on Marine Drive. The BC Hydro EV app and PlugShare show which chargers are free right now.

blocks.text: What public charging costs

parts.t: BC Hydro bills by the kilowatt hour. Since April 1, 2026 the rates are:

items.t: Fast chargers (25 kW and up): $0.3969 per kWh
Level 2 chargers: $0.3083 per kWh
Idle fee at fast chargers: $0.40 a minute, starting five minutes after charging stops
GST of 5% is added to all of it

parts.t: A 40 kWh top-up at a fast charger, roughly half a battery on many EVs, comes to about $16.67 with GST. You pay through a BC Hydro EV account and app, and the same app works at several other networks, including FLO, ChargePoint and Shell Recharge, for a small roaming fee. Rates are on
BC Hydro's charging rates page

blocks.text: Charging at a detached house

parts.t: With a garage or driveway, a Level 2 charger on a 240-volt circuit is the usual answer, installed by a licensed electrician with a permit. Before you buy, check the size of the electrical service: an older home with 100-amp service may need a panel upgrade or a load-management device to add a charger alongside a heat pump or hot tub. BC Hydro has offered a rebate on home chargers; amounts and funding change, so check its site before you order. My post on
CleanBC rebates for home upgrades
covers the other rebates worth stacking.

blocks.text: Buying a condo or townhome: can you charge there?

parts.t: This is where buyers get caught. A parking stall with an outlet nearby is not the same as a stall you're allowed to charge at. BC changed the Strata Property Act to make charging easier, and three things matter.

blocks.text: 1. You have the right to ask, and the strata has to answer

parts.t: An owner can make a written request for a charger, with a description of the equipment, the location and an electrician's estimate of the work and cost. The council must decide within three months and cannot unreasonably refuse. A real shortage of electrical capacity is a valid reason to say no. The strata can require you to pay for the installation, sign an agreement with reasonable conditions, and pay a user fee for the electricity if a bylaw or rule sets one. The rules are set out on the
Province's strata EV charging page

blocks.text: 2. Buildings can now approve charging with a simple majority

parts.t: Since December 6, 2023, a strata needs only a majority vote, not three-quarters, to spend from its contingency reserve on EV charging infrastructure or to change common property for it. A special levy still needs a three-quarters vote.

blocks.text: 3. The electrical planning report tells you what the building can handle

parts.t: Every strata with five or more lots in Metro Vancouver and the Fraser Valley must have an electrical planning report by December 31, 2026. It sets out the building's electrical capacity, its current demand, and what it would take to add EV charging and heat pumps. It is a permanent strata record, and it must be provided with the Form B information certificate when a buyer asks for it. Details are on the
Province's electrical planning report page

blocks.text: What to ask before you write an offer

items.t: Is there already a charger at the stall, or EV-ready wiring to it?
Is the stall part of the strata lot, limited common property or only assigned? An owner who pays for a charger on a common property stall can be given exclusive use for up to five years at a time.
Has the building done its electrical planning report, and what does it say about spare capacity?
Are there bylaws or rules on EV charging and a user fee for the power?
Do the minutes mention an EV project or a levy to pay for one?

parts.t: I read the strata documents for every condo and townhome my buyers consider, and this is now on my standard list.

blocks.text: Rebates for strata buildings

parts.t: BC Hydro's EV Ready rebates for apartment, condo and townhome complexes can cover a large share of a building-wide project:

items.t: EV Ready plan: up to 75% of the cost, to a maximum of $3,000
EV Ready infrastructure: up to 50%, to $600 a parking stall and $120,000 a project
Chargers: up to 50%, to $1,400 a charger in an EV Ready building or $2,000 for a standalone charger, and $14,000 a complex

parts.t: The complex must have five or more units and have been built by August 31, 2022, and the strata needs pre-approval before any work starts. Funding is offered while it lasts. See
BC Hydro's rebates for apartment and condo buildings
. For sellers, a parkade that is already EV Ready is a selling point worth putting in the listing.

blocks.text: Common questions
Can a strata refuse an EV charger in BC?

parts.t: Only with a good reason, such as not enough electrical capacity. The council has to decide within three months of a complete written request and cannot refuse unreasonably.

blocks.text: Who pays for the charger in a condo?

parts.t: Usually the owner who asks for it. The strata can require payment of the installation cost in advance, and can charge a reasonable fee for the electricity used.

blocks.text: How much does it cost to fast-charge in South Surrey?

parts.t: At BC Hydro's chargers, $0.3969 per kWh plus GST since April 1, 2026, so about $16 to $17 for 40 kWh.
